candidates.citation_display: Omnibus Rules Implementing the Labor Code, SECTION 3
candidates.heading: Hours worked
candidates.display_text:
SECTION 3. Hours worked. — The following shall be considered as compensable hours worked:

(a) All time during which an employee is required to be on duty or to be at the employer's premises or to be at a prescribed work place; and

(b) All time during which an employee is suffered or permitted to work.

candidates.heading: Hours Worked
candidates.display_text:
ART. 84. Hours Worked. – Hours worked shall include (a) all time during which an
employee is required to be on duty or to be at a prescribed workplace; and (b) all time during
which an employee is suffered or permitted to work.

Rest periods of short duration during working hours shall be counted as hours worked.

candidates.citation_display: Omnibus Rules Implementing the Labor Code, SECTION 4
candidates.heading: Principles in determining hours worked
candidates.display_text:
SECTION 4. Principles in determining hours worked. — The following general principles shall govern in determining whether the time spent by an employee is considered hours worked for purposes of this Rule:

(a) All hours are hours worked which the employee is required to give his employer, regardless of whether or not such hours are spent in productive labor or involve physical or mental exertion.

(b) An employee need not leave the premises of the work place in order that his rest period shall not be counted, it being enough that he stops working, may rest completely and may leave his work place, to go elsewhere, whether within or outside the premises of his work place.

(c) If the work performed was necessary, or it benefited the employer, or the employee could not abandon his work at the end of his normal working hours because he had no replacement, all time spent for such work shall be considered as hours worked, if the work was with the knowledge of his employer or immediate supervisor.

(d) The time during which an employee is inactive by reason of interruptions in his work beyond his control shall be considered working time either if the imminence of the resumption of work requires the employee's presence at the place of work or if the interval is too brief to be utilized effectively and gainfully in the employee's own interest.

candidates.citation_display: PD 442, as amended and renumbered, ART. 83
candidates.heading: Normal Hours of Work
candidates.display_text:
ART. 83. Normal Hours of Work. – The normal hours of work of any employee shall not
exceed eight (8) hours a day.
Health personnel in cities and municipalities with a population of at least one million
(1,000,000) or in hospitals and clinics with a bed capacity of at least one hundred (100) shall
hold regular office hours for eight (8) hours a day, for five (5) days a week, exclusive of time
for meals, except where the exigencies of the service require that such personnel work for six
(6) days or forty-eight (48) hours, in which case, they shall be entitled to an additional
compensation of at least thirty percent (30%) of their regular wage for work on the sixth day.
For purposes of this Article, "health personnel" shall include resident physicians, nurses,
nutritionists, dieticians, pharmacists, social workers, laboratory technicians, paramedical
technicians, psychologists, midwives, attendants and all other hospital or clinic personnel.72

claims.text: Because the cinema makes ticket staff count their cash drawers before they can clock‑in, the staff are required to be at the employer’s premises and ready for work before their official start time. Under the hours‑worked rule, any time an employee is required to be on duty or to be at a prescribed workplace counts as compensable work time, regardless of whether actual work is performed. Therefore, the pre‑clock‑in cash‑counting activity is considered working time for a covered employee.

paragraphs.text: If the cinema makes ticket staff count their cash drawer before they can clock‑in, that activity is considered working time because the employee is required to be on the employer’s premises and to be ready for duty. Both the Omnibus Rules and the Labor Code state that all time when an employee must be at the prescribed workplace (or is suffered or permitted to work) is compensable, and the principle that any hour the employer requires the employee to give, even if not yet performing the main job, counts as hours worked. Therefore, the cash‑counting task is covered as working time unless the employer can show it is truly voluntary and not a condition of employment.

Because the cinema makes ticket staff count their cash drawers before they can clock‑in, the staff are required to be at the employer’s premises and ready for work before their official start time. Under the hours‑worked rule, any time an employee is required to be on duty or to be at a prescribed workplace counts as compensable work time, regardless of whether actual work is performed. Therefore, the pre‑clock‑in cash‑counting activity is considered working time for a covered employee.
